summary: Changes the IETF standards process in RFC 2026, cutting the standards track from three maturity levels to two. It is a Best Current Practice. The aim is to make advancing a specification simpler and to reflect how the process was already working in practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Almost every RFC the IETF publishes stops at Proposed Standard and stays there. Very few reach the top of the ladder, and the intermediate step in between rarely helps. This document cuts the ladder from three rungs to two and drops the paperwork that had not been happening anyway, so that what counts is whether the specification is actually deployed and working.

subtitle: The IETF standards track goes from three maturity levels to two, and annual review is dropped.

tldr.problem: Documents had trouble advancing through Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Standard, and most stayed at Proposed Standard. Very few advanced in the last decade.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6410 merges Draft Standard and Standard into one level, Internet Standard. Advancement is judged by widespread deployment of independent implementations, and the annual review is dropped.
tldr.outcome: The standards track has two levels, Proposed Standard and Internet Standard. This BCP updates RFC 2026.

facts.label: Maturity levels
facts.value: Two: Proposed Standard and Internet Standard

facts.label: Levels before
facts.value: Three: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Standard

facts.label: Draft Standards may be reclassified
facts.value: at any time after two years from approval

today: RFC 6410 is a Best Current Practice, numbered BCP 9, published in October 2011. It updates RFC 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document changes the Internet Standards Process defined in RFC 2026. In recent years the IETF witnessed difficulty advancing documents through the maturity levels: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and finally Standard. The changes are designed to simplify the Standards Process and reduce impediments to standards progression while preserving the most important benefits of the IETF engineering approach. In addition, the requirement for annual review of Standards Track documents that have not reached the top of the maturity ladder is removed.

Over the years there have been many proposals for refining the Standards Process to reduce impediments to standards progression. During May 2010 the IESG discussed many of these proposals. Then a plenary discussion at IETF 78 in July 2010 demonstrated significant support for transition from a three-tier maturity ladder to one with two tiers.

Experience with a Proposed Standard is expected to motivate revisions that clarify, modify, enhance or remove features. However, in recent years the vast majority of Standards Track documents are published as Proposed Standards and never advance to a higher maturity level, and very few specifications have advanced on the maturity ladder in the last decade. Changing the Standards Process from three maturity levels to two is intended to create an environment where lessons from implementation and deployment experience are used to improve specifications.

The primary aspect of the change is to revise the requirements for advancement beyond Proposed Standard. RFC 2026 requires a report that documents interoperability between at least two implementations from different code bases as an interim step, Draft Standard, before a specification can be advanced further to the third and final maturity level, Standard, based on widespread deployment and use. In contrast, this document requires measuring interoperability through widespread deployment of multiple implementations from different code bases, thus condensing the two separate metrics into one.

The result is expected to be maturity-level advancement based on achieving widespread deployment of quality specifications. The change will also result in the incorporation of lessons from implementation and deployment experience, and recognition that protocols are improved by removing complexity associated with unused features. Since widespread deployment is essentially the metric used for advancement from Draft Standard to Standard in RFC 2026, using the same metric for advancement beyond Proposed Standard means there is no longer a useful distinction between the top two tiers, and the ladder is reduced to two tiers. The requirement for annual review of specifications that have not achieved the top maturity level is no longer required.

This document cuts the ladder from three rungs to two and drops the paperwork that had not been happening anyway, so that what counts is whether the specification is actually deployed and working.

sections.title: Two Maturity Levels
sections.content:
This document replaces the three-tier maturity ladder defined in RFC 2026 with a two-tier maturity ladder. Specifications become Internet Standards through a set of two maturity levels known as the Standards Track. These maturity levels are Proposed Standard and Internet Standard.

A specification may be, and indeed is likely to be, revised as it advances from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard. When a revised specification is proposed for advancement, the IESG shall determine the scope and significance of the changes to the specification and, if necessary and appropriate, modify the recommended action. Minor revisions and the removal of unused features are expected, but a significant revision may require that the specification accumulate more experience at Proposed Standard before progressing.
sections.plainLanguage: The track now has two rungs: Proposed Standard and Internet Standard. A document is expected to change as it climbs, and the IESG decides whether the changes are small enough to allow it to move straight away, or whether it needs more time at Proposed Standard first.

sections.title: The Second Maturity Level: Internet Standard
sections.content:
This maturity level is a merger of Draft Standard and Standard as specified in RFC 2026. The chosen name avoids confusion between Draft Standard and Internet-Draft. The characterization of an Internet Standard remains as described in RFC 2026: an Internet Standard is characterized by a high degree of technical maturity and by a generally held belief that the specified protocol or service provides significant benefit to the Internet community.

The IESG, in an IETF-wide Last Call of at least four weeks, confirms that a document advances from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard. The request for reclassification is sent to the IESG along with an explanation of how the criteria have been met. There are four criteria. There are at least two independent interoperating implementations with widespread deployment and successful operational experience. There are no errata against the specification that would cause a new implementation to fail to interoperate with deployed ones. There are no unused features in the specification that greatly increase implementation complexity. And if the technology required to implement the specification requires patented or otherwise controlled technology, then the set of implementations must demonstrate at least two independent, separate and successful uses of the licensing process.

After review and consideration of significant errata, the IESG will perform an IETF-wide Last Call of at least four weeks on the requested reclassification. If there is consensus for reclassification, the RFC will be reclassified without publication of a new RFC. In a timely fashion after the expiration of the Last Call period, the IESG shall make its final determination and notify the IETF of its decision via electronic mail to the IETF Announce mailing list. No changes are made to Section 6.1.2 of RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet Standard is the top rung, and it merges what used to be two. To get there, a document needs at least two independent implementations that are widely deployed and have worked in practice, no errata that would break a new implementation, no unused features that add a lot of complexity, and, where patents are involved, at least two separate successful licensing arrangements. The IESG then runs a Last Call of at least four weeks. If there is consensus, the existing RFC is reclassified and no new one is published.

sections.title: Transition to Two Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Any protocol or service that is currently at the Proposed Standard maturity level remains so. Any protocol or service that is currently at the Standard maturity level shall be immediately reclassified as an Internet Standard.

Any protocol or service that is currently at the abandoned Draft Standard maturity level will retain that classification, absent explicit actions. Two possible actions are available. A Draft Standard may be reclassified as an Internet Standard as soon as the criteria in Section 2.2 are satisfied. And at any time after two years from the approval of this document as a BCP, the IESG may choose to reclassify any Draft Standard document as Proposed Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing documents are moved over: anything at Standard becomes an Internet Standard, and anything at Proposed Standard stays where it is. The abandoned middle rung is left alone for now, with two ways out: it can be promoted to Internet Standard once it meets the criteria, or, after two years from the approval of this document, the IESG may push it back down to Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Removed Requirements
sections.content:
The requirement for annual review is dropped. In practice, the annual review of Proposed Standard and Draft Standard documents after two years, called for in RFC 2026, has not taken place, and the lack of this review has not revealed any ill effects on the Internet Standards Process. As a result the requirement is dropped, and no review cycle is imposed on Standards Track documents at any maturity level.

The requirement for interoperability testing reporting is dropped as well. Testing for interoperability is a long tradition in the development of Internet protocols and remains important for reliable deployment of services. The IETF Standards Process no longer requires a formal interoperability report, recognizing that deployment and use is sufficient to show interoperability. Although no longer required by the IETF Standards Process, RFC 5657 can be helpful to conduct interoperability testing.
sections.plainLanguage: Two requirements are removed. The annual review of documents that had not yet reached the top rung is dropped, because it had not been happening and nothing bad came of it. The formal interoperability report is dropped too, since real deployment already shows that two implementations interoperate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document does not directly affect the security of the Internet. It changes the process by which a specification is reviewed and promoted, and the requirements for that promotion, rather than the technical content of any specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has no direct effect on the security of the Internet. It changes how documents are reviewed and labelled, not what they say.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CRITERIA FOR INTERNET STANDARD

items.title: Two independent implementations
items.text: With widespread deployment and successful operational experience.

items.title: No harmful errata
items.text: No errata that would make a new implementation fail to interoperate with deployed ones.

items.title: No unused complexity
items.text: No unused features in the specification that greatly increase implementation complexity.

items.title: Licensing
items.text: Where patented or controlled technology is needed, at least two independent and successful uses of the licensing process.
